[0] everyday_reading (E): In English, Total, total and TOTAL are the same word, and names may contain spaces or hyphens (max-value). Java identifiers are case-sensitive and may use only letters, digits, _ and $, so total and Total are different names and max-value is a subtraction.
[1] misconception (M) -> IdentifierCaseInsensitive: wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.
[2] misconception (M) -> NoReservedWords: wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> IdentifierCaseInsensitive: Points to LT (a name refers to the declaration with exactly that spelling in scope). Applied unevenly, a student treats Count and count as one variable in one statement but as two in another. (here mixing in: "System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method")

[0] names_the_element (N): Identifier: a name for a variable, method or class, made of letters, digits, _ and $ and not starting with a digit.
[1] states_the_rule (S): An identifier is a sequence of letters, digits, _ and $ whose first character is not a digit. Identifiers are case-sensitive, and reserved words such as int, public or class cannot be used.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): When an identifier appears, the compiler looks it up by exact spelling among the declarations in scope (an error if none matches). At run time a variable's name is replaced by that variable's current value.
[1] output_prediction (OP): An identifier used as an expression yields the current value of the variable it names, with that variable's declared type. abc, Ab$, abc123 and a_b are legal names; Ab*, 1abc and a+b are not.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): A name does nothing at run time. Only an assignment (or ++ or op=) with the name on its left changes the variable it names.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Each variable is named by one identifier, which must be unique within its scope: declaring a second local with the same name in that scope is a compile error.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A declaration binds the identifier to a type. Every later use must repeat exactly that spelling, or the compiler cannot resolve it.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Identifiers let code refer to values and code by name. Descriptive names make each variable's role readable to people, though names have no effect on what the program computes.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> IdentifierCaseInsensitive: Renaming an identifier consistently at its declaration and every use leaves behavior unchanged. Renaming only some occurrences, or changing only the capitalization, breaks compilation with 'cannot find symbol'.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Identifiers are case-sensitive and must match a declaration exactly; a name that matches nothing in scope cannot be resolved. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Any use whose spelling or capitalization differs from the declaration or library name (Sytem, prinln, Println, studentTotl): compiler reports 'cannot find symbol'.
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Every variable, method and class needs an identifier. Pick descriptive lowerCamelCase names, and use single letters only for short-lived loop indices or standard maths symbols. A name never stands in for a value; only literals and expressions do that.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Every variable must be declared (with a type) before use and referred to by exactly the declared name, inside its scope. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Use of a name that was never declared, was declared under another name, or is used outside the block where it was declared: 'cannot find symbol' (one missing declaration can produce several errors).
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Reserved words cannot be used as identifiers. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Naming a variable new, class, int, public and so on: '<identifier> expected' or 'not a statement'.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: An identifier may not start with a digit or contain spaces or operator symbols. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Names like 2ndValue, max value or max-value: syntax errors, or max - value parsed as a subtraction.
